title: Bounds, skipping and leaving a loop
goal: Explain distinct control paths for stopping and skipping, and confirm them with separate boundary tests.

prerequisites.text: Distinguish a known repetition count, a sentinel and end of input.
Understand ordered checks and independent counters.

terms.title: continue
terms.definition: Finishes this iteration. In a for loop the advance expression then runs before the condition check.

terms.title: Record limit
terms.definition: The maximum number of lines the program considers, including skipped lines.

terms.title: Boundary
terms.definition: A value at which behaviour changes. Test the transition and its neighbours.

sections.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: When reading a queue, some entries must be skipped, while a command can stop all reading. A skipped ticket has already been read, so inspected lines and accepted items are different counters.
In a for loop with ++seen, continue skips the rest of the current body and proceeds to ++seen. break also skips that advance and moves execution after the loop. return ends the function.
Keep guards readable by checking stream end and errors first, then commands, ranges and finally calculations.
Keep three boundaries separate. The record limit ends reading, the marker stops immediately, and a skipped record allows another inspection when the limit still permits one.

sections.title: Classifying a short ticket queue
paragraphs: The example inspects at most five lines. 0 is an empty ticket, −1 ends reading and ticket numbers from 1 to 20 contribute to the sum.
For 0, 0, 3 and −1 on separate lines, predict which iterations skip the calculation and when ++seen runs.
steps: Put the limit in the for header.
Check the read status before using ticket.
A −1 stops traversal. A 0 executes continue.
Only valid tickets change the sum and accepted.

sections.title: Keep the boundary and meaning of counters separate
paragraphs: A limit based on accepted would allow arbitrarily many empty tickets. seen advances in the for header, so skipped records still consume their share of the limit.
The hot threshold includes 30. Using > 30 would differ for a reading of exactly 30. Write tests for 29 and 30 before debugging.
continue belongs in a loop. The compiler rejects it in main with no enclosing loop.

sections.title: Use different tests for different contracts
paragraphs: Six skipped lines followed by a valid seventh line distinguish a scan limit from a measurement limit. A single reading of 30 tests whether the threshold is inclusive.
Also test an invalid record after a valid value. The contract requires only invalid, with no partial summary.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Compare for advancement with continue and break.

selfcheck.prompt: After two lines of 0 and before line 3, what are seen and accepted?
feedback: The for step ran twice. No ticket was accepted.
continue does not skip the for advance.
An empty ticket is not accepted.

selfcheck.prompt: Which single value distinguishes > 30 from the required >= 30?
feedback: Both variants reject 29 for the hot count.

selfcheck.prompt: What should happen with six lines of −99 and 32 on a seventh line? Why?
selfcheck.feedback: Six skipped lines consume six steps without increasing count. The seventh line is not read. The output is empty.

practice.title: Temperatures with skips and a scan limit
practice.task: Read at most six records, one per line. Skip −99. Stop at 999 or EOF. Ordinary temperatures run from −40 to 60 inclusive. On an error, print invalid without a partial summary. If no readings were accepted, print empty. Otherwise print three space-separated integers: the accepted count, their sum, and the count at or above 30. Ignore input after termination.
practice.hint: Put continue for −99 before the range check. Use >= 30 and check that ++seen belongs in the for header.
criteria: A skipped line uses one scan slot without affecting the summary.
Ignore a seventh line and stop early at 999.

steps.action: Mark the action for each record.
steps.why: A stop signal, skip code and measurement follow different paths.
steps.expected: The trace shows seen and count separately.

steps.action: Fix the −99 skip and the boundary 30.
steps.why: The two discrepancies have different causes.

steps.action: Test six skipped records and a seventh line.
steps.why: This checks a limit on scanning.
steps.expected: Print empty and ignore the seventh line.

exercises.title: Module transfer task
exercises.task: Choose your own stream with a stop signal, a skip, 29 and 30. Record seen, count, sum and hot before each step and compare your trace with the output.
criteria: The trace explains termination, the skip and the boundary.
Manual calculation confirms the sum and number of hot readings.
A separate run with an invalid record confirms that there is no partial summary.

cases.label: Every line skipped and limit reached
Above range after a valid reading
Six readings and an extra line

teaching.scene: A dispatcher reviews a queue with blank tickets and a separate stop command. Track two counts: how many records were seen and how many belong in the report.

predict.prompt: The sample receives 0, 0, 3 and −1. What happens to the accepted count at each record, and which two numbers print?
predict.answer: Both zeros take continue and leave accepted at 0. The 3 raises accepted to 1 and sum to 3. −1 ends processing. The output is 1 3.

apply.prompt: The queue starts with five zeroes, then 6. With a five-record inspection limit, does the program reach 6, and what result follows?
apply.answer: Five zeroes consume all permitted inspections. The 6 is left unread. The example model would print 0 0.

practice.strategy: Make a table for errors, stopping, skipping and normal readings. Keep inspected and accepted counts separate, and count values at or above 30 after accepting them.
practice.diagnosis: If −99 produces invalid or changes the sum, check that skipping precedes the ordinary range guard and every report update.

syntax.explanation: continue ends the current iteration. A for loop then advances its inspection counter. The accepted count beyond continue remains untouched.
syntax.mistake: Incrementing the accepted count before the skip test can corrupt the report even when the sum is right.
